sections.h2: No New Hampshire tax on the gain
sections.html:
New Hampshire does not tax the gain from selling a house. The state has no income tax on an individual's reported W-2 wages, and its Interest and Dividends Tax has been repealed.

That leaves three other layers to plan for. The federal government taxes gain on a home sale unless an exclusion covers it, New Hampshire charges a real estate transfer tax on the sale itself, and property tax is settled at closing. For a firm answer on your own return, call the Department of Revenue Administration Taxpayer Services Call Center at (603) 230-5920 or ask a tax professional. This guide is general information.

  • State: no income tax on wages, Interest and Dividends Tax repealed
  • State: real estate transfer tax on the sale, paid by both sides
  • Federal: capital gain tax on any gain above the home sale exclusion
  • Local: property tax prorated or paid at closing

sections.h2: The Interest and Dividends Tax is gone
sections.html:
The Interest and Dividends (I&D) Tax applied to interest and dividend income, and it was repealed for taxable periods beginning after December 31, 2024. It was never a tax on the sale price of a home. People confuse it with a capital gains tax because it was New Hampshire's only tax that reached investment income.

Taxable periodI&D Tax rate
Ending before December 31, 20235 percent
Ending on or after December 31, 20234 percent
Ending on or after December 31, 20243 percent
Beginning after December 31, 2024Repealed

The repeal is covered in Technical Information Release 2025-001, and the law sits in RSA 77 and Rev 900. If you still need to file a final I&D return for an earlier period, those returns go through the state's Granite Tax Connect portal.

sections.h2: How does the federal home sale exclusion work?
sections.html:
If you sell your main home, you can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. You have to pass both an ownership test and a use test.

You meet the ownership test if you owned the home for at least 24 months out of the five years before the sale. You meet the use test if you lived in it as a residence for at least 24 months of those five years. The two periods do not have to be the same 24 months. On a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test.

  • You generally cannot claim it if you excluded gain on another home during the two years before this sale.
  • If you receive Form 1099-S, you must report the sale even if all the gain is excludable.
  • Report on Form 8949 and Schedule D when required.
  • Military, Foreign Service and intelligence-community members on qualified extended duty can elect to suspend the five-year period for up to 10 years.
  • Publication 523 has the full rules, worksheets and exceptions.

An installment sale does not remove the exclusion. It stays available even if you spread the gain over later years.

sections.h2: Federal rates on gain above the exclusion
sections.html:
A gain on a home held more than one year is long-term and is taxed at 0, 15 or 20 percent for most sellers, depending on taxable income. A gain on a home held a year or less is short-term and taxed as ordinary income.

For taxable years beginning in 2025, a single filer pays 0 percent up to $48,350, 15 percent from $48,350 to $533,400, and 20 percent above $533,400. A married couple filing jointly pays 0 percent up to $96,700, 15 percent from $96,700 to $600,050, and 20 percent above $600,050.

A few exceptions apply. The part of a gain tied to unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property is taxed at a maximum of 25 percent, which can matter if you rented the house and took depreciation. People with significant investment income may also owe the net investment income tax, and a large gain can call for estimated tax payments.

If you sell a personal home at a loss, the loss is not tax deductible.

sections.h2: Inherited or improved homes: figuring the gain
sections.html:
Gain is the amount you realize from the sale minus your adjusted basis. Basis is generally your cost, plus improvements that add value, minus items such as allowable depreciation.

If you received the property by gift or inheritance, basis is figured under different rules, and Publication 551, Basis of Assets, covers them. Get a date-of-death value from an appraisal and keep it with the estate papers. A tax preparer will ask for that record.

  • Improvements: new roof, additions, major systems. Keep receipts.
  • Selling costs: ask your preparer which closing costs reduce the amount realized.
  • Holding period: property acquired from a decedent has special holding-period rules, covered in Publication 544.

The real estate transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price or consideration, and both the buyer and the seller pay it. For a sale of $4,000 or less, each side pays a $20 minimum.

The tax is governed by RSA 78-B and Rev 800. Buyer and seller buy stamps from the register of deeds in the property's county, and the register attaches them to the deed when it is recorded.

Within 30 days after the deed is recorded, both parties file their Declaration of Consideration (CD-57-P for the purchaser and CD-57-S for the seller) and the Inventory of Property Transfer (PA-34) with the state. Filing and payment can be done through Granite Tax Connect.

  • Taxable: sales, foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu, sheriff's sale deeds, leases of 99 years or more
  • Exempt: gifts, transfers between spouses under a final divorce decree, corrective deeds, transfers to the state, a county or a municipality, and transfers by devise, intestate succession or a joint tenant's death

sections.h2: Property tax in a New Hampshire sale
sections.html:
The property tax year runs April 1 to March 31 under RSA 76:2, and taxes are assessed on the April inventory. Whoever owns the house on April 1 appears on the assessment, and the closing agent settles the split between buyer and seller.

Late taxes carry 8 percent interest under RSA 76:13. If a municipal tax lien is recorded, RSA 80:69 sets 14 percent interest per year on the lien and lets anyone with a legal interest in the land redeem it before the collector gives a deed. The sale proceeds usually clear it through the title company.

For city specifics, our Manchester and Nashua guides cover those offices and dates.

sections.h2: Before you sell with a large gain
sections.html:
Work out your basis and your exclusion before you sign, because those two numbers decide whether any federal tax is due. A seller who lived in the house for two of the last five years and has a gain under $250,000 may owe nothing federally, though reporting is still required in some cases.

  1. Gather the purchase closing statement and improvement receipts.
  2. Count your months of ownership and residence in the last five years.
  3. Check whether a 1099-S will be issued.
  4. Ask a preparer about estimated tax if a taxable gain is likely.
  5. Budget for the 0.75 percent transfer tax on your side.

A cash sale does not change these rules. It changes the timeline, so you can plan when proceeds arrive against any estimated tax payment your preparer expects. Bring the closing statement from your purchase, your improvement receipts and any tax notices to that first conversation with a preparer.

faqs.q: Does New Hampshire have a capital gains tax?
faqs.a: No state tax applies to gain from a home sale. New Hampshire has no income tax on W-2 wages, and the Interest and Dividends Tax was repealed for periods beginning after December 31, 2024. Federal tax can still apply.

faqs.q: How much gain can I exclude on a house sale?
faqs.a: Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home for at least 24 months of the last five years. The exclusion is barred if you used it on another home in the prior two years.

faqs.q: Who pays the New Hampshire real estate transfer tax?
faqs.a: Both buyer and seller pay it, at $0.75 per $100 of the price. Transfers by will, intestate succession and a joint tenant's death are exempt.

faqs.q: Do I report a home sale if I owe no tax?
faqs.a: Yes, if you receive Form 1099-S, you must report the sale even when the gain is excludable. You also report it if you cannot exclude all the gain.

faqs.q: Is a loss on a personal home deductible?
faqs.a: No. Losses from the sale of personal-use property, such as your home, are not tax deductible.
